newsitem.title: USA: PacifiCare stock tumbles on earnings warning.
newsitem.headline: PacifiCare stock tumbles on earnings warning.

text.p: Shares of PacifiCare Health Systems Inc. tumbled more than 20 percent Tuesday after the managed health care company said its second-quarter results would fall substantially below analysts' estimates.

While some analysts responded to the warning by reducing earnings estimates for the company, others waited cautiously for more information, saying the uncertainty could be worse than the actual shortfall.

PacifiCare Class B shares lost $20.125, or 23.5 percent, to $65.375 in heavy trading on Nasdaq, where it was one of the biggest losers and among the most active issues with more than 5.4 million shares traded in late trading. Its class A shares fell $17.875 or about 22 percent to $63.125, also on Nasdaq.

Cypress, Calif.-based PacifiCare issued a statement late Monday that its earnings for the three months ending June 30 would be "substantially below" consensus estimates of $1.16 a share. But it then declined to elaborate on the extent of the shortfall, leaving many investors guessing.
In the comparable year-ago quarter the company had net income of $8.57 million, or 27 cents a share.

PacifiCare, one of the nation's largest health maintenance organisations, blamed the earnings shortfall on the poor performance of FHP International Co., which it acquired for $2.2 billion in February, and on disappointing results in its core California market for the month of May.
A PacifiCare spokeswoman said Tuesday the company would not reveal any more information about its earnings expectations until later in the week.

"Uncertainty is probably the worst thing you can have with a stock," said Alex Brown analyst Eleanor Kerns. "They just said they expect to miss their quarter and will have more details later. That leaves people with no information to deal with."
But other analysts estimated the shortfall would between 10 cents and 20 cents a share off earnings for the quarter.
"There is real potential here for significant misses in the FHP California and the non-California business," said Robertson Stephens analyst Thomas Hodapp.
"California is a very competitive market. Unlike much of the rest of the country, it has not had strong premium increases."

Because the HMO business is more mature in California than in the rest of the country, managed care companies seeking to attract new enrollees in the state have been under severe pressure to limit premium increases.

In addition, many analysts said the task of integrating the operations of FHP has proven to be daunting to PacifiCare. Many of FHP's markets, like Colorado, Ohio, Utah and New Mexico, have seen especially sharp increases in medical costs.

"FHP had been positioning itself to be sold for two years and had not focused a lot of time on marketing and expense mangement," said Hambrecht and Quist analyst Ken Laudan. "PacifiCare has excellent management but it won't be able to turn this great titanic around any time soon."
But Laudan added the PacifiCare warning could be an early sign of more troubles for the rest of the managed care industry, which has long been plagued by cost pressures.
Increasingly, these companies are at a loss to find new ways to save money, he said.
"Relying heavily on utilization reductions like shorter hospital stays just doesn't provide the same returns it used to," Laudan said. "These companies are seeing diminishing returns."
